summary:
MARSWALK is a walking-scale traverse planner for a single real place on Mars: the boxwork ridges on Mount Sharp in Gale crater, where Curiosity examined boxwork formations in 2025. It visualizes the site in 3D using NASA terrain and orbital images, enabling an astronaut to plan a science walk of up to six stops, then try out the path eye-to-eye with a simulated view of Curiosity's photos, prior to departure from the habitat.
It tackles the challenge by stacking data from multiple NASA missions: Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Mars Odyssey, Curiosity, and Mars Global Surveyor. These help MARSWALK drill down to optical, thermal, topographic, and radiation information. Each segment is planned two ways - a faster route and a safer one - accounting for slope and terrain to steer clear of hazards. MARSWALK then confirms that both crew members can see each other in daylight conditions and with NASA's forecast solar storms in mind, and accounts for how crew members can communicate if one is in shade. MARSWALK's field guide notes whether each figure is measured, calculated, estimated, or simulated.
That's important because the initial crews on Mars will require hyperlocal, reliable information rather than broad global maps. Providing safety, conditions and science objectives in one reliable, honestly and clearly communicated perspective, MARSWALK demonstrates how current mission data can enable humans to reach, explore and work on Mars efficiently, safely and effectively.
details:
MarsWalk

What it does

The first people to walk on Mars will not need a map of the planet. They will need a map of the next five hundred meters. MarsWalk is a walking-scale traverse planner and field guide for one real place on Mars: the boxwork ridges on lower Mount Sharp in Gale crater, where NASA’s Curiosity rover drilled in 2025. It turns orbital images, a 1 meter terrain model and Curiosity’s own records into a plan an astronaut could follow: where to walk, how long it takes, whether it is safe to go, and what they will see. It runs as a single web page on a laptop or phone, with no installation and no account.

How it works: the user experience

A story that sets the scene. A first visit opens a nine-chapter scroll story. A globe of Mars turns to Gale crater, the camera descends to the boxwork, and the story hands the user to the planner. “Skip to the planner” goes straight there.

Plan a science walk. The planner shows a 3 by 3 km area of real terrain in 3D. A default walk runs from the edge of the boxwork to the Monte Grande hollow and the Nevado Sajama ridge that Curiosity drilled, and back. Users add up to six stops by clicking the ground, dragging a beacon, or choosing from 114 real places where Curiosity stopped for three sols or more. “Quickest order” reorders the stops, and four ready-made plans are one click away.

Two routes for every leg. Direct is fastest. Cautious accepts a longer walk to avoid steep ground. Both stay under an adjustable slope limit (20 degrees by default). Users compare time, distance, climb and the share of steep ground, then choose.

A GO or NO-GO call. MarsWalk checks that the walk leaves after sunrise, returns with at least an hour of daylight to spare, and keeps every step within the slope limit. For a pair, it also checks that the astronauts stay within 300 meters of each other and out of sight for no more than ten minutes at a time. Any failure turns the call to NO-GO and says why. A daylight timeline lets users drag the departure time and watch the call change, and NASA space weather forecasts add a caution if a solar storm is due within a day.

Work in pairs. Pair mode splits the stops between astronauts A and B, routes both, and checks their separation and line of sight over the ridges every half minute.

See the data. A Data layers panel lists each dataset with its source and toggles overlays: slope hazard, night surface temperature, Curiosity’s drive path, the planning boundary, terrain relief, and a clearly labelled Mars color tint. Hovering reads out slope and height.

Science sites with real photos. Every site card shows a real Curiosity Navcam photo. Ten sites carry notes written from NASA’s Curiosity mission blog, five of them drill sites.

Walk it at eye level. Users can follow the route at human height, at half speed to four times speed. The walk pauses at each stop with Curiosity’s photo, and a visor shows the next stop or hazard, time left and back-by time. A helmet view and a clickable height profile are included.

A printable field guide. A one-page crew briefing includes the objective, a route map on HiRISE imagery, a timeline with arrival times, sun angle, cumulative radiation dose and height at each stop, turn-back times, a leg-by-leg plan, conditions, and the limits of the data. Every number is labelled measured, derived, assumed or simulated.

How it works: the data and the engine

NASA data (all public, no keys needed):

  • Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter HiRISE imagery (about 0.7 m per pixel) via Mars Trek, as the base map.
  • USGS Mars MSL Gale Merged DEM, 1 m (Parker and Calef, 2016), used for slope and routing. It merges HiRISE, CTX and ESA Mars Express HRSC stereo data.
  • MRO CTX mosaic for the surroundings, and Mars Odyssey THEMIS night-time infrared for the surface temperature layer.
  • Curiosity waypoints, traverse, REMS weather records, RAD radiation measurements (about 0.67 mSv per day) and Navcam images.
  • NASA DONKI solar storm forecasts, the Viking MDIM 2.1 color mosaic for the globe, and the NASA GISS Mars24 algorithm for sun position, checked to within a minute of Curiosity’s measured sunrise and sunset.

The engine. Terrain is resampled to a 2 m grid and slope is computed with the Horn method. Walking speed follows Tobler’s hiking function, scaled so flat ground gives 2.5 km/h, matching NASA’s Apollo planning figure for suited walking. Routes are found with A* search on an 8-connected grid, blocked above the slope limit, then straightened without crossing steeper ground. Routing runs in a Web Worker so the interface never freezes. Radiation dose is the RAD rate multiplied by time outside, and line of sight between partners is traced over the terrain from eye height.

Benefits

  • Grounded in real data. Every route is computed on NASA’s actual terrain, at a site Curiosity has explored.
  • Honest about what it knows. Each figure states its source. Assumptions are labelled and adjustable, and a limits section lists what the data cannot see, such as rocks smaller than about 1 meter.
  • A complete decision. It answers what a crew asks before going outside: which way, how long, how steep, back before dark, safe to go, and what is at each stop.
  • Rehearsal before risk. Crews can see the ridges, climbs and turn-back points before anyone suits up.
  • Accessible. One file, works offline, runs on phones, and respects reduced-motion settings.

Intended impact

MarsWalk shows how existing NASA data can be combined to plan the first human steps on Mars at the scale people actually walk. For mission planners, it is a template for turning orbital and rover data into routes, limits and a GO or NO-GO call. For future crews, it is a way to rehearse an EVA on real terrain. Because it only needs a HiRISE-scale terrain model, the method can be applied to any candidate site. For students and the public, it makes one real place on Mars something anyone can walk, and it teaches how to read data honestly.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: TypeScript for the app, Python 3 for the data pipeline, HTML and CSS.
  • App: three.js 0.186 for 3D, a Web Worker for routing, and Vite with vite-plugin-singlefile to build everything into one self-contained HTML file.
  • Data pipeline: Python with NumPy, Rasterio and Pillow to clip the terrain model, fetch tiles, find Curiosity’s stops, choose Navcam photos, and compute sun geometry and ambient occlusion.
  • Testing: Vitest (22 engine tests, including route search checked against brute-force Dijkstra) and Playwright (42 browser checks), plus oxlint.
  • Fonts and icons: B612 and B612 Mono, Instrument Serif, Phosphor icons.
  • Hardware: the team’s own laptops. Collaboration was on GitHub.
  • AI assistance: Claude Code helped draft documents and write code. The concept, framework and decisions are the team’s, and we reviewed what it produced. The demo video was assembled with Claude from real footage and carries a visible AI-assisted watermark.

How it is creative

  • Walking scale, not planet scale. It is built around the next few hundred meters, the distance a person in a suit actually covers.
  • A decision tool with a story. A cinematic scroll takes users from the whole planet to one ridge before handing over the controls.
  • Two routes, a call, and a rehearsal. This is an end-to-end crew workflow, not a map viewer.
  • Pairs and line of sight. Staying close and in view is a real EVA rule that maps rarely model.
  • Curiosity as a scout. The rover’s real stops, photos and drill sites become the stations a human crew would visit next.
  • Provenance as a feature. Labelling every number is part of the design, not a footnote.

Factors the team considered

  • Science objective: why the boxwork ridges resisted erosion while the hollows did not. A person on foot could sample several ridge and hollow pairs in one walk.
  • Site choice: Gale is the only place on Mars with a surface radiation detector and a weather station, and it has 1 meter terrain data and published ground truth.
  • Human limits: suited walking speed, slope limit, daylight reserve, time at each stop, and radiation dose.
  • Pair safety: separation and line of sight between partners.
  • Data honesty: no invented numbers. Every figure is traced to a source or labelled as assumed, and known gaps are stated, including no route-scale radiation map and no dust or sand modelling.
  • Scope: one real site done thoroughly rather than a thin planner for anywhere.
  • Performance and accessibility: tiled terrain with four detail levels, baked shading, a Performance mode, a phone layout, reduced motion and plain English.
  • Rules and licensing: Apache 2.0, third-party licenses listed, credits for every NASA dataset, no NASA logos or insignia, and AI use disclosed.

MarsWalk

What it does

The first people to walk on Mars won’t need a map of the planet. They’ll need a map of the next five hundred meters. That’s what MarsWalk is: a walking-scale traverse planner and field guide for one real place on Mars, the boxwork ridges on lower Mount Sharp in Gale crater, where Curiosity drilled in 2025. We took orbital images, a 1 meter terrain model and Curiosity’s own records and turned them into a plan an astronaut could follow. It tells you where to walk, how long it takes, whether it’s safe to go, and what you’ll see when you get there. It’s a single web page that runs on a laptop or phone, with no install and no account.

How it works for the user

It starts with a story. when you open it, you scroll through nine short chapters. A globe of Mars turns to Gale crater, the camera drops down to the boxwork, and then the story hands you the controls. If you’d rather skip it, there’s a “Skip to the planner” button.

You plan a science walk. The planner shows a 3 by 3 km patch of real terrain in 3D. You can add up to six stops by clicking the ground, dragging a beacon, or picking from 114 real places where Curiosity stayed for three sols or more. “Quickest order” shuffles your stops into the shortest sequence, and four ready-made plans are one click away.

Every leg gets two routes. Direct is the fastest. Cautious takes a longer way around to avoid steep ground. Both stay under a slope limit you can adjust (20 degrees by default). You compare time, distance, climb and how much steep ground each one crosses, then pick.

You get a clear GO or NO-GO. MarsWalk checks that the walk starts after sunrise, finishes with at least an hour of daylight left, and never exceeds the slope limit. For two astronauts, it also checks that they stay within 300 meters of each other and are never out of sight for more than ten minutes at a stretch. If anything fails, the call flips to NO-GO and tells you why. A daylight timeline lets you drag the departure time and watch the verdict change, and NASA space weather forecasts add a warning if a solar storm is due at Mars within a day.

Pairs work together. Real EVAs are done in pairs, so pair mode splits the stops between astronauts A and B, routes both, and checks their distance and line of sight over the ridges every half minute.

You can see the data. A Data layers panel lists every dataset with its source and lets you switch overlays on the terrain: slope hazard, night surface temperature, Curiosity’s drive path, the planning boundary, relief, and a Mars color tint (labelled as a tint, since the orbital images are greyscale). Hover anywhere to read the slope and height.

Science sites come with real photos. Every site card shows an actual Curiosity Navcam photo taken there. Ten sites also have notes drawn from NASA’s Curiosity mission blog, with links to the posts. Five of those are drill sites.

You can walk it at eye level. This puts you on the ground at human height, following your route at anywhere from half speed to four times speed. It pauses at each stop with Curiosity’s photo, and a visor shows the next stop or hazard, time left and back-by time. There’s also a helmet view and a height profile you can click to jump around.

You can print a field guide. It’s a one-page crew briefing with the objective, a route map on HiRISE imagery, a timeline (arrival times, sun angle, cumulative radiation dose and height at each stop), turn-back times, a leg-by-leg plan, conditions, and the limits of the data. Everything comes from public NASA and partner data, and no keys are needed:

  • HiRISE imagery from Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (about 0.7 m per pixel), through Mars Trek, as the base map.
  • The USGS Mars MSL Gale Merged DEM at 1 m (Parker and Calef, 2016), which we use for slope and routing. It combines HiRISE, CTX and ESA Mars Express HRSC stereo data.
  • An MRO CTX mosaic for the surroundings, and Mars Odyssey THEMIS night infrared for the surface temperature layer.
  • Curiosity’s waypoints and traverse, REMS weather records, RAD radiation measurements (about 0.67 mSv per day) and Navcam images.
  • NASA DONKI solar storm forecasts, the Viking MDIM 2.1 color mosaic for the globe, and the NASA GISS Mars24 algorithm for the sun’s position, which we checked against Curiosity’s measured sunrise and sunset and which agrees to within a minute.

Under the hood, we resample the terrain to a 2 m grid and compute slope with the Horn method. Walking speed comes from Tobler’s hiking function, scaled so flat ground works out to 2.5 km/h, which matches NASA’s Apollo planning figure for suited walking. Routes are found with A* search on an 8-connected grid, blocked above the slope limit, then straightened without crossing steeper ground. Routing runs in a Web Worker so the page never freezes. Benefits

MarsWalk is grounded in real places and real data. Every route is computed on NASA’s actual terrain, at a site Curiosity has explored. It’s also honest about what it knows. Each figure names its source, assumptions are labelled and adjustable, and a limits section spells out what the data can’t see, like rocks smaller than about a meter.

It gives a complete decision rather than just a map. It answers what a crew would ask before stepping outside: which way, how long, how steep, will we be back before dark, is it safe, and what’s at each stop. And it lets a crew rehearse. Walking the route at eye level shows the ridges, climbs and turn-back points before anyone suits up. It’s one file, works offline, runs on phones, and respects reduced-motion settings.

Intended impact

We wanted to show how existing NASA data can be combined to plan the first human steps on Mars at the scale people actually walk. For students and the public, it makes one real place on Mars something anyone can walk, meter by meter, and it shows how to read data honestly.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: TypeScript for the app, Python 3 for the data pipeline, plus HTML and CSS.
  • App: three.js 0.186 for 3D, a Web Worker for routing, and Vite with vite-plugin-singlefile to bundle everything into one self-contained HTML file.
  • Data pipeline: Python with NumPy, Rasterio and Pillow, used to clip the terrain model, fetch tiles, find Curiosity’s stops, pick Navcam photos, and compute sun geometry and ambient occlusion.
  • Testing: Vitest (22 engine tests, including route search checked against brute-force Dijkstra) and Playwright (42 browser checks), plus oxlint.
  • Fonts and icons: B612 and B612 Mono, Instrument Serif, and Phosphor icons.
  • Hardware and collaboration: our own laptops, with GitHub for teamwork.
  • AI assistance: Claude Code helped us draft documents and write code. The concept, framework and decisions are ours, and we reviewed everything it produced. We assembled the demo video with Claude from real footage of the app, and it carries a visible AI-assisted watermark.

How it’s creative

  • Walking scale, not planet scale. Most Mars maps show regions. MarsWalk is built around the few hundred meters a person in a suit can actually cover.
  • A tool with a story. A cinematic scroll takes you from the whole planet down to one ridge before you take over.
  • A full crew workflow. Comparing a fast and a cautious route, getting a verdict, then walking it at eye level goes well beyond a map viewer.
  • Pairs and line of sight. Staying close and in view is a real EVA rule that maps rarely model.
  • Curiosity as a scout. The rover’s real stops, photos and drill sites become the stations a human crew would visit next.
  • Provenance as a feature. Labelling every number is part of the design, not a footnote.

Factors we considered

  • Science objective: why the boxwork ridges resisted erosion while the hollows didn’t. Curiosity drilled one of each a month apart, and a person on foot could sample several pairs in a single walk.
  • Site choice: Gale is the only place on Mars with a surface radiation detector and a weather station, and it has 1 meter terrain data and published ground truth.
  • Human limits: suited walking speed, slope limit, daylight reserve, time at each stop and radiation dose.
  • Pair safety: distance and line of sight between partners.
  • Data honesty: no invented numbers. Everything is traced to a source or labelled as assumed, and the gaps are stated: no route-scale radiation map, no walking-scale thermal data, no rocks under about a meter, and no dust or sand modelling.
  • Scope: we chose one real site done thoroughly over a thin planner for anywhere on Mars.
  • Performance and accessibility: tiled terrain with four detail levels, pre-baked shading, a Performance mode for weaker devices, a phone layout, reduced-motion support and plain English.
